bioluminescence.title: Bioluminescence
bioluminescence.description: The biochemical emission of light by living organisms. It has evolved independently dozens of times — recent estimates put it at more than 90 separate origins across bacteria, fungi, and animals.

showdown.detail: Oxidise luciferin in a specialised lantern organ, flashing species-specific codes to attract mates.
Emits a continuous green glow, likely to attract insects that help disperse its spores.
Doesn't make its own light at all — its lure is packed with symbiotic glowing bacteria.

camera_eye.title: The Camera Eye
camera_eye.description: A hollow eye with a lens that focuses light onto a retina. This complex structure evolved completely independently in vertebrates and cephalopods.

showdown.detail: Our retinal wiring sits in front of the light receptors, creating a blind spot where the optic nerve exits.
Their wiring sits behind the receptors. Same camera design, but with no blind spot.

echolocation.title: Echolocation
echolocation.description: Navigating and hunting by emitting sound and listening for echoes. Bats and toothed whales arrived at it separately — and even share convergent changes in the same hearing gene, prestin.

showdown.detail: Produce ultrasonic calls in the larynx and catch echoes with large, mobile ears.
Generate clicks in their nasal passages, focus them through the fatty 'melon', and hear echoes through the lower jaw.

electroreception.title: Electroreception
electroreception.description: Sensing the faint electric fields produced by other animals' muscles and nerves. It has been lost and re-invented several times among vertebrates.

showdown.detail: Jelly-filled pores called ampullae of Lorenzini let them find prey buried in sand.
Tens of thousands of receptors in its bill let it hunt underwater with its eyes, ears and nostrils shut.
Go a step further: they sense fields and generate discharges of several hundred volts.

eusociality.title: Eusociality
eusociality.description: Societies with a reproductive caste, sterile workers, and overlapping generations. It evolved separately in ants, in bees, in termites — and even in naked mole-rats.

showdown.detail: Colonies of tens of thousands coordinate foraging through the 'waggle dance'.
Some species maintain fungus farms, herd aphids, and build living bridges from their own bodies.

flight.title: Powered Flight
flight.description: Flapping flight evolved at least four separate times: in insects, pterosaurs, birds, and bats — each building a wing from different parts.

showdown.detail: Stretch a thin membrane across hugely elongated finger bones.
Use feathers anchored to fused hand bones; a stooping peregrine exceeds 300 km/h.
Insect wings aren't modified limbs at all, but outgrowths of the exoskeleton.

photosynthesis.title: Photosynthesis
photosynthesis.description: A trick question! Plants didn't evolve photosynthesis on their own — their chloroplasts descend from cyanobacteria that an ancestor engulfed. Shared machinery, borrowed rather than convergent.

showdown.detail: Invented oxygen-producing photosynthesis and oxygenated Earth's atmosphere.
Run the same reactions inside chloroplasts, which still carry their own bacterial DNA.

silk_production.title: Silk Production
silk_production.description: Protein fibres spun from liquid into solid thread. Spiders and many insects make silk using entirely unrelated glands.

showdown.detail: Spin from abdominal spinnerets and can produce up to seven kinds of silk for different jobs.
Moth larvae spin cocoon silk from modified salivary glands near the mouth.

tool_use.title: Tool Use
tool_use.description: Using external objects to achieve a goal. Once thought uniquely human, it has turned up in primates, birds, marine mammals and even molluscs.

showdown.detail: New Caledonian crows craft hooked tools from twigs to fish grubs out of wood.
Veined octopuses carry coconut shell halves to assemble into a shelter later.
Some wear marine sponges on their snouts to protect them while foraging on the seafloor.

venom.title: Venom
venom.description: Toxins delivered through a wound. Venom has evolved independently more than 100 times across the animal kingdom.

showdown.detail: Fire a harpoon-like modified tooth loaded with fast-acting neurotoxins.
Males carry venomous spurs on their hind legs — one of very few venomous mammals.
Deliver venom through long, hinged fangs that fold away when the mouth closes.
